references.text: God breathed the breath of life (nishmat chayyim) into man's nostrils – exactly the same expression as in Gen 7:22, where everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. The gift of life from creation is reversed in the flood.
God warns that He will bring the flood to destroy all flesh that has the breath of life (ruach chayyim), the same expression used in 7:22 when judgment is executed.
The previous verse describes how all flesh that moved on the earth perished – the immediate context for the statement in verse 22.
Verse 23 summarizes the destruction: all living things were wiped out from the earth; only Noah and those with him in the ark were spared.
Psalm 104 describes God's sovereign control over the breath of life: when He takes it away, creatures die – the same principle as in Gen 7:22.
Isaiah urges not to trust in man who only has breath (neshama) in his nostrils – an allusion to human frailty demonstrated in the flood.
Hebrews highlights Noah's faith as the reason he and his family were saved from the judgment that struck all living things in Gen 7:22.
Job 34:15 theologically anchors the historical judgment in Genesis 7:22 as an expression of God's sovereign right to take life when all flesh returns to dust.
Genesis 8:19 completes the narrative by showing restoration after the total death described in 7:22, emphasizing God's plan for both judgment and renewal.
